title: Business Component
description: A business component is the product, process, software, technique, formula or invention to which the IRC § 41(d)(2) four-part test is applied separately.
summary: A business component is the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to which U.S. taxpayers must separately apply the four-part test under IRC § 41(d)(2) to claim the federal R&D tax credit. Because at least 80% of each component's activities must form a process of experimentation, defining components narrowly and tracking costs at that level is essential.

body.text: A business component is the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to which U.S. taxpayers must separately apply the four-part test under IRC § 41(d)(2) to claim the federal R&D tax credit. Because at least 80% of each component's activities must form a process of experimentation, defining components narrowly and tracking costs at that level is essential.
Executive Summary and Statutory Architecture of the Business Component

The Business Component (BC) constitutes the foundational unit of statutory analysis for substantiating claims under the United States Research and Development (R&D) Tax Credit, codified at Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41). Rather than evaluating research and development eligibility at the enterprise level or across broad corporate capital initiatives, IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) mandates that the four-part statutory qualification test be applied separately to each discrete business component developed or improved by the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), a business component is defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Consequently, every dollar of claimed Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—encompassing in-house wages and supplies under IRC § 41(b) and Treasury Regulation (Treas. Reg.) § 1.41-2, as well as eligible contract research expenditures—must be directly linked to a properly delineated business component.

The strategic and legal significance of the business component boundary arises from the structural interaction between two regulatory mechanisms: the "Substantially All" rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) and the "Shrink-Back" rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Because at least 80% of the research activities undertaken with respect to a defined business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose, defining a component too broadly introduces severe examination exposure. When routine engineering, commercial adaptation, user-interface styling, or post-production activities dilute the proportion of qualified experimentation below the 80% threshold, the entire component fails statutory qualification unless the taxpayer can systematically narrow—or "shrink back"—the unit of analysis to a qualifying subset of elements supported by granular, contemporaneous cost and time records.

This structural interaction creates a critical compliance dynamic wherein accounting architecture directly dictates substantive tax eligibility. A taxpayer performing genuine scientific experimentation can forfeit its entire credit claim not from a lack of qualifying engineering activity, but from a mismatch between how engineering teams track project budgets and how tax regulations define a business component. Enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems and capital budgeting protocols typically aggregate labor and material costs under overarching commercial initiatives, customer contracts, or product lines. When those high-level cost centers are imported uncritically into an R&D tax credit study as single business components, the denominator of the 80% fraction swells with non-qualifying support tasks, triggering total disallowance of the experimental core unless sub-component financial records exist to substantiate a narrower boundary.

Regulatory enforcement of component-level substantiation has intensified significantly with the revision of Internal Revenue Service (IRS) Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. January 2025). Optional for the 2024 tax year and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2024, the revised Form 6765 requires taxpayers to identify and classify the specific business components generating at least 80% of total claimed QREs (up to a maximum of 50 components) and to disclose the technical information sought to be discovered for each component. Consequently, component delineation has evolved from a retrospective audit-defense exercise conducted after return filing into a mandatory pre-filing compliance architecture that must be embedded into engineering and financial governance from project inception.
Definitional Scope and Component Separation Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)
The Six Statutory Categories and the Commercial Nexus Requirement

IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) establishes six exhaustive categories of business components: products, processes, computer software, techniques, formulas, and inventions. While "product" and "process" address tangible goods and operational or manufacturing workflows, the statutory inclusion of "technique," "formula," and "invention" extends qualification to intangible technical methodologies, chemical or material compositions, and patentable or proprietary engineering designs, provided the underlying activities satisfy the four-part qualification test. This taxonomic breadth ensures that research credits are not restricted to traditional heavy manufacturing, accommodating modern technological development across biotechnology, specialty chemicals, algorithmic systems, and precision automation.

Each business component must satisfy a dual commercial-use nexus under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B): the taxpayer must intend either to hold the component for sale, lease, or license to third parties, or to use the component in the active conduct of the taxpayer's own trade or business. This trade or business requirement also governs the underlying research expenditures under IRC § 41(b), ensuring that purely academic or non-commercial inquiry falls outside the credit's ambit. However, IRC § 41(b)(4) provides a critical statutory exception for certain startup ventures whereby in-house research expenses are treated as paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business if the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making such expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business. Without this statutory bridge under IRC § 41(b)(4), pre-revenue biotechnology, clean-tech, and hardware startups developing their inaugural product or formula business component would be barred from claiming in-house wage and supply QREs prior to commercial launch.

body.text: Product Versus Process Separation Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C)

A foundational structural rule in R&D tax compliance is the mandatory separation of production processes from the products they manufacture. Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) ("Special rule for production processes"), any plant process, machinery, or technique for commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component, and not as part of the business component being produced. This provision is not merely a permissive accounting election; it is a mandatory statutory partition designed to prevent the cross-contamination of qualification metrics between product engineering and manufacturing engineering.

Analytical evaluation of IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) demonstrates why conflating product design with manufacturing process engineering frequently destroys otherwise valid claims during IRS examinations. In complex industrial environments, a product's design may already be fully established—meaning product-level activities face minimal technological uncertainty—while scaling that product to commercial manufacturing tolerances introduces profound uncertainty regarding machinery shear limits, thermal dynamics, automated calibration, or throughput speeds. If the taxpayer fails to isolate the production process as a discrete business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and instead aggregates process trials with routine commercial production of the established product, the routine product activities will overwhelm the denominator of the 80% "Substantially All" calculation and disqualify the process engineering expenses. Conversely, a novel product formulation may require extensive laboratory experimentation to resolve chemical stability uncertainty, whereas packaging that formulation on an existing assembly line involves only routine mechanical setup. By isolating the "process BC" from the "product BC" under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C), taxpayers prevent routine activities in one domain from diluting the 80% "Substantially All" calculation of the other. As confirmed by Tax Court jurisprudence, including the analysis referenced in Stephens, the initial classification and boundary definition between product and process components directly govern both the evidentiary burden of substantiation and the computation of allowable QREs.
Statutory Exclusions Bounding Component Eligibility

Even where a valid business component exists, IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and IRC § 41(d)(4) expressly exclude specific categories of activities from qualifying as research. When defining the scope of a business component and tracking associated costs, taxpayers must segregate and remove these excluded activities to prevent contamination of the component's qualification ratio. Specifically, under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), any activity conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component is disqualified unless a separate process of experimentation is initiated to develop a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality, or a separate production process component is being developed under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C). This commercial production cutoff requires clear documentation of when pre-production prototyping ends and commercial manufacturing begins, particularly when trial production runs occur on full-scale factory equipment.

Similarly, IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) excludes any research related to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. If a technical modification is engineered solely to fulfill a specific client contract—such as configuring an existing software platform to interface with a client's legacy database or resizing a mechanical valve to fit a customer's facility footprint—without resolving a broader technological uncertainty applicable to a new or improved business component for general commercial application, it fails statutory qualification. The statute also bars efforts aimed at reproducing existing technical designs. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C), any research related to duplicating an existing business component, in whole or in part, from a physical examination of the component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information is non-qualifying. While developing a novel manufacturing process to produce a generic equivalent can qualify as a separate process or formula component if existing specifications do not disclose the formulation or production method, reverse-engineering a competitor's product from blueprints or physical teardown is statutorily barred.

Furthermore, IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) explicitly excludes non-technical and routine operational activities, including efficiency surveys, activities relating to management functions or techniques, market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions), routine data collection, and routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control. Finally, under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), research conducted for purposes relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors fails the qualified purpose test even if engineering or scientific tools are utilized during execution. In consumer packaged goods, food science, and industrial design, this requires strict segregation between sensory taste panels or aesthetic packaging redesigns (excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)) and hard-science formulation trials aimed at microbial shelf stability, structural integrity, or chemical dissolution rates (qualified under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)).
Application of the Four-Part Qualification Test to Each Business Component

Under IRC § 41(d)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4, a taxpayer must demonstrate that activities mapped to each business component satisfy four cumulative tests, with the business component acting as the analytical anchor for all four prongs. Failure to satisfy any single prong at the defined component level necessitates either shrinking back to a narrower qualifying sub-component under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) or abandoning the claim for that component altogether.
The Qualified Purpose Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and Section 41(d)(3))

Research activities must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information whose application is intended to be useful in the development of a new or improved business component of the taxpayer. Under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A), the purpose counts as qualified only if it relates to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality of the business component. Notably, the statutory standard is taxpayer-specific rather than industry-wide: the functional or technical improvement must be new to the taxpayer, not necessarily new to the broader industry. Provided the taxpayer does not have access to publicly available blueprints, formulas, or detailed specifications that would trigger the duplication exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(C), independent experimentation to achieve a functional or performance benchmark already attained by a competitor satisfies the qualified purpose requirement.
The Technological in Nature Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(B)(i))

The process of discovering information for the business component must be technological in nature, meaning it must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. This requirement distinguishes qualified technical investigation from activities rooted in social sciences, economics, business management, market research, or subjective intuition. While utilizing computer-aided design (CAD), finite element analysis, simulation tools, or algorithmic modeling helps demonstrate reliance on engineering or computer science principles, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) clarifies that the taxpayer may employ existing scientific principles and is not required to expand or refine the underlying body of common knowledge within a field of science. The analytical focus rests on whether hard-science principles govern the investigative methodology applied to the specific business component.
The Elimination of Technological Uncertainty Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(a)(3))

Activities must be intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(3), uncertainty exists if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component. This tripartite regulatory framework—capability uncertainty, method uncertainty, and appropriate design uncertainty—is essential for evaluating industrial and software R&D. Crucially, even if the taxpayer knows with certainty that it is technically possible to achieve a functional objective (capability) and understands the general engineering methodology to pursue (method), qualifying technological uncertainty still exists if the appropriate design of the business component remains unknown at the project's inception. Conversely, if the required design can be determined through standard, routine engineering calculations on existing data or by communicating known parameters to an architect, vendor, or technician, technological uncertainty is absent and the activity fails IRC § 41(d)(1)(A).
The Process of Experimentation Test (IRC Section 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(a)(5))

Substantially all of the activities undertaken for the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5), a process of experimentation is a systematic process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. To satisfy this standard under IRS examination, the taxpayer's technical records must demonstrate a rigorous three-part evaluative progression: first, identifying the specific uncertainty regarding the development or improvement of the business component; second, identifying one or more technical alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and third, identifying and conducting a systematic process of evaluating those alternatives through modeling, simulation, hypothesis testing, prototyping, or systematic trial and error. Simple iterative arithmetic calculations, unguided debugging, or routine validation checks do not constitute an evaluative process of experimentation. However, because statutory eligibility turns on the investigative purpose and scientific methodology rather than commercial success, research activities satisfy the four-part test even if the technical effort ultimately fails to produce a commercially viable business component.
The Substantially All Mandate and Strategic Application of the Shrink-Back Rule
Mechanics of the 80% Substantially All Threshold

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement is satisfied only if 80% or more (≥ 80%) of a taxpayer's research activities for a given business component—measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (such as employee hours)—constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. The remaining 20% or less (≤ 20%) of activities may consist of directly supporting or supervising activities that do not themselves constitute core experimentation, provided they are not statutorily excluded activities.

This 80% threshold creates a binary, all-or-nothing qualification cliff at the defined component level. When a taxpayer defines an entire commercial project (for example, "Project Alpha" or "The Analytics Platform 2.0") as a single business component, routine coding, user-interface styling, standard mechanical assembly, vendor integration, and post-production testing are swept into the denominator of the 80% calculation. If non-qualifying activities exceed 20% of total component activities—dropping qualified experimentation below 80%—the component fails the "Substantially All" test in its entirety, resulting in 0% qualification at that hierarchical level.
The Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(b)(2))

To prevent total forfeiture of legitimate research expenses when an overarching product or process fails the four-part test, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) establishes the Shrink-Back Rule. Under this regulation, the four-part test is applied first at the level of the discrete product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in its trade or business. If the requirements of IRC § 41(d) are not met at that initial level—most commonly because routine engineering activities dilute the experimentation ratio below 80%—the test is then applied to the most significant subset of elements of the product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention. This shrinking-back continues iteratively to smaller subsets until either a subset of elements of the business component that satisfies the statutory requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and fails to satisfy the requirements.

cells: Complete commercial product or capital project (e.g., "The Car" or "Analytics Platform 2.0").
High Risk: Overly broad scope sweeps routine assembly and commercial tasks into the denominator, causing failure of the 80% Substantially All test.
Medium Risk: Narrower boundary improves technical focus, but mixed routine and experimental subsystem tasks may still dilute the 80% ratio.
Discrete technical element or algorithm (e.g., "Fuel Injection Algorithm" or "NLP Query Parser").
Low Risk: Highly specific boundary isolates technological uncertainty and maps directly to the four-part test and process of experimentation.

body.text: An inherent operational tension—characterized as the "Specificity Paradox"—governs R&D credit claims across these hierarchical levels. Claiming an entire product or overarching capital project maximizes the nominal pool of gross expenses (indexed at 100 in relative claim size), but yields an estimated 10% probability of IRS audit acceptance because routine implementation, integration, and commercial tasks inevitably push the qualified experimentation ratio below 80%. Narrowing the component definition to a major subsystem raises audit acceptance probability to approximately 45% (with a relative claim size index of 60), whereas isolating the specific business component where technological uncertainty actually resided raises audit acceptance probability to 95% (with a relative claim size index of 40). Evaluated on an expected-value basis (Acceptance Probability × Claim Size Index), the specific Level 3 component yields an expected risk-adjusted value of 38.0 (0.95 × 40), nearly quadrupling the expected value of the overly broad Level 1 claim (0.10 × 100 = 10.0) while substantially mitigating examination disallowance risk.

Furthermore, reactive reliance on the Shrink-Back Rule during an IRS examination frequently fails in practice if the taxpayer did not establish sub-component cost accounting from the project's inception. If employee time logs and general ledger accounts record hours only against a high-level project code ("New Bottling Line Project" or "Analytics Platform 2.0"), the taxpayer lacks the evidentiary nexus required to prove what portion of wages belonged to the shrunk-back sub-component ("Star-Wheel Gripper Mechanism" or "NLP Query Parser"). When taxpayers attempt to reconstruct sub-component wage allocations years later through retrospective oral estimates, the IRS and the Tax Court routinely reject those estimates for failing to establish a verifiable nexus between specific employee hours and the shrunk-back business component. Consequently, treating the Shrink-Back Rule as an upfront design protocol—by defining business components at the sub-system, module, or feature level before work begins—is essential to surviving examination scrutiny.
Worked Example 1 (Hypothetical): Monolithic Failure vs. IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) Separation and Shrink-Back

To demonstrate the exact mathematical operation of the 80% "Substantially All" rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)), product-versus-process separation (IRC § 41(d)(2)(C)), and the Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)), consider a hypothetical food and beverage manufacturer, FlavorCorp, developing a new line of shelf-stable, ready-to-eat soup. Suppose FlavorCorp expends 10,000 hours at a blended wage rate of $100 per hour, totaling $1,000,000 in total project wage expenditures across three technical and commercial workstreams. In Workstream A (Formulation of the Reduced-Sodium Flavor Compound, or RSFC), food scientists spend 4,500 hours ($450,000) developing the RSFC, of which 4,050 hours ($405,000) involve systematic thermal treatment trials and chemical assays to resolve uncertainty regarding natural preservative stability under high-temperature commercial retort packaging, while 450 hours ($45,000) involve routine quality-control inspections excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D). In Workstream B (Plant Automation and the Proprietary Automated Ingredient Blending Technique, or AIBT), process engineers spend 3,500 hours ($350,000) upgrading the production line; within this workstream, 2,950 hours ($295,000) are dedicated to experimental modeling and trial runs on the AIBT subsystem to resolve uncertainty regarding mixing shear limits and dynamic flow algorithms for high-viscosity dispersion, 150 hours ($15,000) involve routine AIBT calibration checks, and 400 hours ($40,000) involve installing standard, off-the-shelf conveyor belts and motors. In Workstream C (Sensory Taste Panels and Packaging Market Research), marketing and sensory staff spend 2,000 hours ($200,000) conducting consumer taste panels and packaging design surveys, all of which are statutorily excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) (0 qualified hours).
Scenario 1A: Monolithic Business Component Definition (Failure of the 80% Rule)
If FlavorCorp defines the entire initiative as a single Business Component titled "New Soup Line Project" encompassing all 10,000 hours ($1,000,000), total qualified experimentation hours equal:
Qualified Experimentation Hours = 4,050 + 2,950 + 0 = 7,000 hours

Total non-qualifying hours equal 450 + 550 + 2,000 = 3,000 hours, representing exactly 30.0% of total project hours spent on non-qualifying activities. Applying the "Substantially All" test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) yields:
Monolithic Qualification Ratio = 7,000 hours ÷ 10,000 hours = 70.0%

Because 70.0% < 80.0%, the monolithic "New Soup Line Project" fails the "Substantially All" mandate. Without component separation or sub-component time records to support shrinking back, $0 of the $1,000,000 project expenditure qualifies at the monolithic project level.
Scenario 1B: Bifurcation Under IRC Section 41(d)(2)(C) and Shrink-Back Under Treas. Reg. Section 1.41-4(b)(2)

Suppose instead that FlavorCorp applies IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) to separate the product formulation from the manufacturing process and excludes Workstream C (2,000 hours of taste panels and market research) from its R&D business component definitions. For Business Component 1 (Product BC — Reduced-Sodium Flavor Compound), the qualification ratio is:
BC 1 Qualification Ratio = 4,050 hours ÷ 4,500 hours = 90.0% ≥ 80.0%

BC 1 satisfies the 80% threshold, preserving the $405,000 in qualified formulation wages. Simultaneously, for Business Component 2 (Process BC — Automated Ingredient Blending Technique), when measured across the entire Workstream B plant upgrade (3,500 hours), the qualification ratio is:
BC 2 Broad Process Ratio = 2,950 hours ÷ 3,500 hours = 84.29% ≥ 80.0%

Moreover, even if standard conveyor installation had consumed 650 hours instead of 400 hours—which would have raised Workstream B total hours to 3,750 hours and lowered the broader plant upgrade ratio to 2,950 ÷ 3,750 = 78.67% < 80.0%—granular sub-component tracking allows FlavorCorp to invoke the Shrink-Back Rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) to narrow BC 2 specifically to the AIBT subsystem (3,100 hours):
BC 2 Shrunk-Back AIBT Ratio = 2,950 hours ÷ 3,100 hours = 95.16% ≥ 80.0%
Thus, both BC 1 ($405,000) and BC 2 ($295,000) satisfy the statutory framework, securing $700,000 in base QREs that would have been completely forfeited under a monolithic project definition.

Four industry benchmarks further illustrate how overly broad project descriptions must be narrowed to defensible business components to isolate technical uncertainty across diverse industrial and digital sectors:

body.text: Specialized Compliance for Internal Use Software (IUS) Business Components

When a business component falls within the "computer software" category under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), taxpayers must navigate the specialized regulatory regime governing Internal Use Software (IUS) under IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6). Because modern enterprises devote substantial engineering payroll to proprietary digital infrastructure, correctly classifying software components at the outset of development is one of the highest-stakes determinations in corporate R&D tax planning.
Defining Internal Use Software and General and Administrative Functions

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), software is presumed to be developed primarily for the taxpayer's internal use if it is developed for use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business. G&A functions explicitly include financial management (for example, accounting, financial reporting, and tax compliance), human resources management (for example, payroll, benefits administration, and workforce tracking), and support services (for example, routine internal inventory management, data processing, or facility operations). Whether software constitutes IUS is determined based on the taxpayer's intent and the specific facts and circumstances existing at the beginning of the software development project.

Here again, how the taxpayer defines the boundary of the software business component exerts a decisive operational effect on qualification. If a taxpayer bundles a customer-facing transaction engine together with an internal back-office financial reconciliation module into a single monolithic software business component, the G&A functionality can taint the characterization of the unified software package or force a complex dual-function analysis. Conversely, separating the architecture into discrete microservices or software modules at project inception allows each software business component to be evaluated cleanly under its respective regulatory standard.
Statutory and Regulatory Exceptions to IUS Classification

Software avoids classification as IUS—and therefore bypasses the stringent High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test, requiring only the standard four-part test—if it satisfies one of two primary regulatory exceptions under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6). First, under the Commercial Marketing Exception, software is not considered IUS if it is developed to be commercially sold, leased, licensed, or otherwise marketed to third parties. Second, under the Third-Party Interaction Exception, software is not considered developed primarily for internal use if it is developed to enable a taxpayer to interact with third parties or to allow third parties (such as customers, vendors, or suppliers) to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system.

The Third-Party Interaction exception serves as a major safe harbor for modern digital enterprises, e-commerce platforms, financial technology providers, and Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) architectures. For example, if a manufacturer develops custom web-portal software that allows customers to initiate orders and track shipment or inventory data on the taxpayer's system, that software business component is excluded from IUS treatment and is evaluated solely under the standard four-part test of IRC § 41(d).
The Three-Prong High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) Test

If a software business component is determined to be IUS (such as proprietary enterprise resource planning or internal financial analytics software) and does not qualify for an exception, IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) require the component to satisfy both the standard four-part test and all three cumulative prongs of the High Threshold of Innovation (HTI) test:

cells: The software must be intended to be innovative, meaning it would result in a reduction in cost, improvement in speed, or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant, if development is successful.
Pre-development architecture specifications establishing quantifiable performance benchmarks (e.g., targeted 40% reduction in data-processing latency or 15% operational cost savings).

The software development must involve significant economic risk, meaning the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period.

Capital allocation budgets linked to documented technical risk assessments, architectural feasibility failures, and proof that uncertainty stems from technical capability/design rather than market risk.

The software must not be commercially available for use by the taxpayer, meaning it cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would themselves satisfy the first two prongs (innovation and significant economic risk).

Contemporaneous vendor evaluation matrices and RFPs demonstrating a diligent market search confirming that commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) enterprise software could not fulfill the technical requirements.

body.text: In examination practice, the third prong—Not Commercially Available—represents the most formidable barrier for G&A software claims. Given the breadth of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) enterprise software packages available from major cloud and ERP vendors, taxpayers claiming IUS components must preserve objective, pre-project market gap analyses and request-for-proposal (RFP) evaluations proving why available commercial solutions could not be purchased, leased, or configured without undertaking fundamental computer science experimentation that independently satisfies the innovation and significant economic risk prongs.
IRS Form 6765 Disclosures and Proactive Component-Level Governance
Mandatory Component-Level Reporting on Revised Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025)

The IRS has fundamentally restructured R&D tax credit reporting through revisions to Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, Rev. January 2025). While Section G component-level reporting was made optional for the 2024 tax year, it becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after 2024. Under the revised Form 6765 instructions, taxpayers claiming the credit must identify all business components related to the claimed credit and report the top Business Components in descending order of QRE amount that collectively account for at least 80% of total claimed QREs, capped at a maximum of 50 Business Components. For each reported component, the taxpayer must classify the component by its specific statutory category under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) (product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention), describe the specific information sought to be discovered and the qualified research activities performed, and allocate qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses directly to the corresponding Business Component ID.

This disclosure regime fundamentally alters IRS examination selection and audit dynamics. Rather than filing Form 6765 with only aggregate enterprise-wide wages, supplies, and contract research expenses and deferring component identification until an examination is opened, taxpayers must now present their component architecture on the face of the tax return. By requiring upfront disclosure of the top 80% of QREs by discrete business component (up to 50 components) alongside qualitative descriptions of the information sought to be discovered, Section G enables IRS examiners to screen returns immediately for overly broad component names, post-production activities, customer-adaptation projects, or unsubstantiated IUS claims prior to issuing initial examination requests.
Worked Example 2 (Hypothetical): Form 6765 Top-80% / 50-Component Disclosure Calculation

To illustrate the exact mathematical mechanics of the Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025) component disclosure rule, consider a hypothetical technology and industrial enterprise claiming $2,500,000 in total QREs across eight discrete business components for a tax year beginning after 2024. Under the Form 6765 instructions, the taxpayer must report components in descending order of QREs until cumulative reported QREs reach at least 80% of total QREs, subject to the 50-component ceiling:
Mandatory Itemized Disclosure Threshold = 0.80 × $2,500,000 = $2,000,000

When the taxpayer ranks its eight business components in descending order of QRE expenditure, the largest component, BC-01 (Computer Software — NLP Query Parser), accounts for $750,000 (30.0% of total QREs), bringing the running cumulative total to $750,000 (30.0%). The second-largest component, BC-02 (Product — High-Durability Air Brake System), accounts for $550,000 (22.0% of total QREs), raising the cumulative total to $1,300,000 (52.0%). The third component, BC-03 (Process — CNC Milling Path Optimization Algorithm), adds $425,000 (17.0% of total QREs), bringing the cumulative total to $1,725,000 (69.0%). The fourth component, BC-04 (Formula — Polymer Coating Dissolution Formula), adds $325,000 (13.0% of total QREs), pushing the running cumulative total to $2,050,000 (82.0%). The remaining four minor components (BC-05 through BC-08) represent individual QREs of $150,000, $125,000, $100,000, and $75,000, respectively, totaling $450,000 (18.0% of total QREs).
Verifying the cumulative threshold after including the fourth component (BC-04) confirms compliance:
Cumulative Share of Total QREs = $2,050,000 ÷ $2,500,000 = 82.0% ≥ 80.0%

Because stopping at BC-03 would leave the taxpayer at $1,725,000 (69.0% < 80.0%), the taxpayer must include BC-04 to cross the 80.0% ($2,000,000) threshold. Once BC-04 is included ($2,050,000, or 82.0%), the taxpayer has satisfied the mandatory itemization threshold using four components—well under the 50-component cap—and may report the remaining $450,000 (18.0%) from BC-05 through BC-08 on an aggregate basis in accordance with the Form 6765 instructions.
Strategic Recommendations for Component-Level Audit Readiness

Transitioning from retrospective expense estimation to contemporaneous component-level substantiation requires embedding IRC § 41(d)(2) compliance directly into engineering and financial workflows. First, taxpayers should formalize granular business component definition protocols through an internal tax-and-engineering policy manual that defines components at the sub-system, module, or formula level rather than the overarching commercial product or client contract level, while mandating the automatic separation of commercial production processes from manufactured products under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) at project kickoff.

Second, organizations should integrate contemporaneous uncertainty and experimentation tracking directly into existing R&D project management systems—such as Jira, Asana, Git repositories, or electronic laboratory notebooks—so that technical tickets and employee time logs link directly to a discrete Business Component ID. Within these systems, technical leads should contemporaneously record the specific capability, method, or design uncertainty addressed, the technical alternatives evaluated, and the testing, modeling, or trial-and-error protocol employed, including failed iterations.

Third, prior to preparing Form 6765, tax teams should execute pre-filing "Substantially All" mock audits by measuring qualified experimentation hours and costs against total hours and costs for every defined business component. Where any component falls below the 80% threshold under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6), the taxpayer should immediately execute the Shrink-Back Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)) internally to redefine the component around its qualifying sub-element and segregate non-qualifying routine activities prior to return filing.

Finally, for every software business component, taxpayers must enforce pre-project IUS due diligence by documenting the primary intended use at project inception; if the software supports G&A functions without qualifying for the Commercial Marketing or Third-Party Interaction exceptions, the taxpayer must compile contemporaneous proof of all three HTI prongs—quantifiable innovation targets, technical risk budgets, and a documented market search confirming commercial unavailability—before claiming associated QREs.

body.text: Conclusion

The statutory architecture of IRC § 41(d)(2) elevates the Business Component from a descriptive label to the decisive structural determinant of R&D tax credit validity in the United States. Because the four-part qualification test and the 80% "Substantially All" mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) operate as an all-or-nothing filter at the level of each defined component, an overly broad component boundary allows routine engineering, commercial adaptation, or aesthetic design tasks to invalidate legitimate scientific experimentation. Conversely, disciplined upfront application of product-versus-process separation under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) and sub-component delineation under the Shrink-Back Rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) insulates core experimental activities from dilution and maximizes risk-adjusted credit recovery. With the implementation of mandatory component-level disclosures on Section G of revised IRS Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025) for tax years beginning after 2024, taxpayers can no longer rely on post-filing reconstruction to define their business components. Aligning engineering project management, time-tracking granularity, and general ledger cost accounting with discrete sub-system, process, formula, and software business components at project inception is now an indispensable prerequisite for sustaining R&D tax credits under IRS examination.
